science.title: Large-Scale Image Dataset for Physics Laboratory Equipment Detection Using Deep Learning Models
science.description: Physics laboratory setting has still not been studied seriously in the area of computer vision although it has pedagogical and operational importance. The current research in physics education is limited to simulation or design of activities without a standardized and machine-readable visual representation of the actual laboratory equipment. We address this gap by providing a filtered set of physics laboratory equipment that has been experimented under realistic conditions at United International University, Dhaka. We have recorded 5121 images taken by four camera devices with different specifications consisting of 27 equipment categories with 8700 high quality annotations. Both bounding-box and polygon tools are used to label every image to provide geometric accuracy. The dataset can be used to train and benchmark deep learning models to detect equipment, where YOLOv8 and YOLOv11 have mean average precisions (mAP@50) of 85.4% and 86.4%, respectively. In addition to research, the dataset will allow its practical implementation in safety in laboratories, automatic tracking of the inventory, and feedback systems to improve education. This work contributes to a fundamental resource connecting artificial intelligence and learning experimental science by presenting the first open dataset of detecting physics lab equipment.

science.title: In 2016, scientists identified the globe skimmer as the world's longest-distance insect flyer. Years later, it reshaped our understanding of insect migration
science.description: Researchers from Rutgers University have uncovered genetic evidence demonstrating that dragonflies embark on remarkable long-distance migrations. These agile insects are capable of traversing thousands of miles over oceans, utilizing their wings to ride on weather currents for long durations. By aligning their journey with seasonal weather shifts, dragonflies seek out the essential moisture needed for reproduction. This groundbreaking find positions dragonflies as the world's premier long-distance migrators.
